transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. [Name]. It's nice to meet you. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, well, the main reason I came in is that I just get pulled off track so easily. Like, I'll be working on something for school—I'm a sophomore, by the way, majoring in communications, which is actually super interesting because we're learning about media theory right now, and my professor used to work in PR for this huge tech company, so she has all these crazy stories. But anyway, yeah, I'll be trying to finish a project, and then one Slack ping goes off, or I hear a song lyric, or I get a random idea for something completely different, and suddenly I’ve just totally lost the thread of what I was supposed to be doing. It's really frustrating.
How long have you been experiencing these difficulties with staying focused and getting distracted? Have you always had trouble with this, or is this something that started more recently?

Um, well, I guess it hasn't always been this bad. It really started causing real problems for me about a year and five months ago. That was when I kind of transitioned from just doing my regular, structured school projects into trying to build up my own freelance UX and data-visualization portfolio on the side. 

Because, you know, with school, the professors basically tell you exactly what to do and when it's due. But with the portfolio, it's all on me. And I got super into UX design—I actually started redesigning our campus dining app for my first case study because the current one is just awful. Like, if you try to check the weekend hours for the café, the whole thing just crashes. Every single time. My roommate literally had to order pizza twice last week because she couldn't figure out if the dining hall was open. So I was teaching myself Figma to try and redesign it, which is this really cool collaborative design tool, and then I was also looking at Tableau for the data-viz stuff because I love infographics and I think data journalism is getting so huge right now... 

Wait, sorry, I'm doing it again. What did you ask me? Oh, right, how long. Yeah, so about a year and five months is when I really noticed it getting hard to manage.

You mentioned that with school projects, the professors tell you exactly what to do and when it's due, and that works better for you. Do you also have trouble staying focused on other things in your life—like when you're with friends, or doing chores at home, or things that aren't work or school-related?

Um, yeah, I definitely have trouble focusing on other stuff too. Like, even with things I actually *want* to do, it’s hard. Like, I can sit down to read a research article for my media theory class, or even just watch a UX tutorial on YouTube—which I love doing, by the way, there's this one channel where the guy breaks down app interfaces and he's so funny, he actually used to be a stand-up comedian before he got into tech, which is such a weird career pivot, right? Like, how do you go from telling jokes in a club to designing wireframes? But I guess a lot of it is about understanding human psychology, which is basically what comedy is... 

But anyway, yeah, I'll be trying to read or watch the tutorial, and after a few minutes, I’ll realize my eyes have just been moving across the page or staring at the screen, and I literally have no idea what I just took in. It’s like my brain just went on a completely different vacation while my body stayed there. And with chores... oh my gosh, laundry is the worst. I'll start a load, and then go to the kitchen to get a snack, and then start organizing the pantry because the cereal boxes are all crooked, and then three days later I realize my wet clothes are still sitting in the washing machine smelling like mildew. It's so embarrassing.
When you're in a quiet room with no phone, no computer, and nothing else around—just you and one task—are you still having trouble focusing, or does that help you stay on track?

Um, you'd think that would help, right? Like, just stripping everything away so there are no distractions. But honestly, it almost makes it worse. Even when I try to do something really relaxing, like reading a book for fun or doing a calm sketching exercise—because I've been trying to get better at hand-drawing wireframes before I move them into Figma. My professor says starting on paper is crucial for the creative process, and she actually showed us her old sketchbooks from when she was working at that tech company, and they were so messy but so brilliant. She used these specific Japanese gel pens, the really fine-point ones, which I actually ordered online last week but they haven't arrived yet because I think there was a shipping delay at the warehouse...

Wait, sorry. The quiet room thing. Yeah, so even when I try to just sit quietly with a sketch or a book, I can't just *be quiet* with it. I end up talking to myself out loud, or I absolutely have to put on music, or I'll suddenly feel this intense need to check something, or I'll take this simple little sketching exercise and turn it into this massive, complicated project. It's like my brain can't handle the silence, so it just creates its own noise.

When you're doing something that you find genuinely interesting and engaging—like working on a UX design project that excites you—can you sit down and work on it for, say, 30 minutes to an hour without your attention drifting away, or does your mind wander even when you're doing something you really enjoy?

Um, yeah, it's honestly exactly like what I was saying just a minute ago about those YouTube videos. Even if it's something I'm super excited about, like a UX tutorial on color theory—which is totally fascinating, by the way. Like, did you know different shades of blue make users trust an app more? That's why basically every bank app is blue. My bank actually just updated their interface last month and the new shade of blue is so aggressive, it's like this neon cobalt. My roommate actually painted her side of our dorm room a color exactly like that and it gives me a headache every time the sun hits it. She calls it "ocean breeze" but it's definitely more like "radioactive waste," and we're probably going to lose our security deposit because you're definitely not supposed to paint the walls in campus housing... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, working for 30 minutes. Yeah, no, even with the fun stuff, I can sit down to read a design article or watch one of those tutorials I actually *want* to watch, and after just a couple of minutes, I'll realize my eyes have just been moving across the screen or the page, and I have absolutely zero idea what I just took in. My mind just drifts right off, no matter how much I like the project.

When you're sitting down trying to work or focus, do you find yourself fidgeting a lot—like bouncing your leg, tapping your fingers, moving around in your chair—or do you feel this restless energy in your body that makes it hard to just sit still?

Um, yeah, all the time. Like, especially in meetings or when we have these portfolio reviews for my design classes. I’m almost always bouncing my leg, or clicking my pen, or twisting my rings around. Actually, I lost one of my favorite rings last week doing that. It was this really cool silver one with a tiny moonstone that I got at a vintage market downtown. The market is so fun, they have all these local artisans and food trucks. There's this one truck that makes the best Korean BBQ tacos, and the line is always like a mile long, but it's totally worth it. The guy who runs it was telling me about how he sources all his ingredients locally, which I think is super important for sustainability. I watched this whole documentary on food supply chains recently and it was honestly terrifying how much waste there is...

But um, yeah, the fidgeting. I don't even realize I'm doing it until someone looks at me weird or asks me to stop clicking my pen. I just shift around in my chair constantly. It's like my body just has to be doing *something* even if I'm supposed to be sitting still.

F98.8 (other behavioral/emotional disorders) is less specific and less supported by this clear ADHD symptom cluster.
